# Genesis 20 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter records Abraham’s second deception regarding Sarah (the first being in Genesis 12:10–20 in Egypt). He tells Abimelech king of Gerar that Sarah is his sister; she is taken into the king’s harem; God intervenes by dream; Abimelech restores Sarah and rebukes Abraham; Abraham prays and the household is healed.

---

## Verse 1

**Now Abraham journeyed from there to the region of the Negev and settled between Kadesh and Shur. While he was staying in Gerar,**

- **Why Abraham moved:** After the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Abraham left Mamre (Gen 18:1). Several suggestions are offered: he sought fresh pasture (Keil), wanted to escape the scene of judgment (Calvin, Murphy), faced hostility from neighbours (Calvin), or wanted to benefit more places by his presence (A Lapide). Some suggest God impelled him to remind him Canaan was for pilgrimage, not permanent settlement (Poole, Kalisch). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- David Guzik notes Abraham may not have wanted to live overlooking the destroyed region and be reminded of the judgment. He also suggests Abraham was operating in unbelief or at least without clear divine direction, given his subsequent actions. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

- **Gerar** was a prosperous Philistine city controlling a caravan route, about 12 miles SE of Gaza, in the land of the Philistines. The name means “lodging place” or “halting place.” Precept Austin notes: “For Abraham, it became a halting place in his walk with God.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-20-commentary)

- JFB notes Gerar’s neighbourhood was “a very rich and well-watered pasture land.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-20.html)

- **Between Kadesh and Shur:** Precept Austin notes Shur means “wall” or “fortification” and comes from a root meaning “to turn or wander about.” This may reflect Abraham’s spiritual condition—drifting, looking around for something better. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-20-commentary)

---

## Verse 2

**Abraham said of his wife Sarah, “She is my sister.” So Abimelech king of Gerar had Sarah brought to him.**

- **A repeated sin:** This is the same deception Abraham used in Egypt (Gen 12:13). The Pulpit Commentary calls it “well nigh unaccountable, and almost irreconcilable with any degree of faith and piety,” given the lapse of 20+ years since Pharaoh’s rebuke and the recent promises about Sarah bearing the promised seed (Gen 17:16). One explanation offered: the earlier “success” (God protected them in Egypt) may have encouraged Abraham to think God would protect them again—though this was “in reality a tempting of God.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik points out that Sarah was about 90 years old. Her attractiveness at this age may be explained by miraculous rejuvenation connected with her receiving strength to conceive (as Morris and Kurtz suggest). More importantly, taking her into a harem may have been a political move: she was connected to a wealthy, influential nomad prince. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

- JFB calls Abraham’s conduct “highly culpable. It was deceit, deliberate and premeditated—there was no sudden pressure upon him—it was the second offense of the kind—it was a distrust of God every way surprising.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-20.html)

- **“Abimelech”** means “father-king” and was a dynastic title of Philistine kings, just as “Pharaoh” was for Egyptian monarchs. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Precept Austin stresses that Abraham’s besetting sin repeated itself: “Age does not automatically sanctify us. Unless yielded to the Spirit of God, we will repeat in our old age the sinful patterns of our youth.” The chapter is about God overruling even our besetting sins to accomplish His kingdom purposes. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-20-commentary)

---

## Verse 3

**One night, however, God came to Abimelech in a dream and told him, “You are as good as dead because of the woman you have taken, for she is a married woman.”**

- **“God” (Elohim):** The Pulpit Commentary notes the entire chapter uses Elohim (except v.18 which uses Jehovah). This is explained by the fact that the chapter describes God’s dealings with a heathen monarch to whom the covenant name YHWH was unknown. The use of Jehovah in v.18 is because it is the covenant God of Sarah who interposes for her protection. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- **Dreams as revelation to pagans:** Dreams were the usual mode of self-revelation by God to non-covenant peoples—compare Pharaoh’s dreams (Gen 41) and Nebuchadnezzar’s (Dan 4). This is distinguished from the higher form of theophanies and visions granted to covenant people like Abraham (Gen 12:7; 15:1; 18:1). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- **“You are as good as dead”** —literally “behold, you are dying” or “about to die” (LXX: σὺ ἀποθνῄσκεις). The Pulpit Commentary suggests Abimelech was already suffering from the malady God had brought upon his household (see v.17). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik: “This was a frightening thing to hear from God, even in a dream.” He quotes Barnhouse: “Suppose Abimelech had taken Sarah and God had not intervened? Two seeds would have been at the door to Sarah’s womb, and to this day an element of doubt would cling to the ancestry of our Lord.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

- JFB: “In early times a dream was often made the medium of communicating important truths; and this method was adopted for the preservation of Sarah.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-20.html)

---

## Verse 4

**Now Abimelech had not gone near her, so he replied, “Lord, would You destroy a nation even though it is innocent?”**

- **“Had not come near her”:** The Pulpit Commentary says Abimelech was apparently withheld by the disease that had overtaken him. This statement was “clearly rendered necessary by the approaching birth of Isaac, who might otherwise have been said to be the child not of Abraham, but of the Philistine king.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- **“Would You destroy a righteous nation?”:** Abimelech anticipates judgment on his whole people and deprecates it, alluding to Sodom’s fate (Knobel). The Pulpit Commentary notes Abimelech and his people—like Melchizedek and his subjects—had some knowledge of the true God and had not sunk to Sodom’s moral degradation. Their comparative virtue demonstrated “the hour had not arrived for the infliction on them of the doom of extermination.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik: “God strongly made the point to Abimelech, even though he could truly say he acted in the integrity of his heart and innocence of his hands.” The drastic warning was necessary because something of cosmic importance was at stake—the purity of the Messianic line. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

---

## Verse 5

**“Didn’t Abraham tell me, ‘She is my sister’? And she herself said, ‘He is my brother.’ I have done this in the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands.”**

- The Pulpit Commentary observes that the Philistine monarch, like the Egyptian Pharaoh before him, “shrank from the sin of adultery.” Abimelech assumed “the right of kings to take unmarried persons into their harems.” He acted in integrity of heart because he was deceived. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- This verse demonstrates that Abimelech was a victim of Abraham’s deceit, not a predator. His appeal to integrity and innocence is accepted by God in the following verse—yet he still needed to make restitution.

---

## Verse 6

**Then God said to Abimelech in the dream, “Yes, I know that you did this with a clear conscience, and so I have kept you from sinning against Me. That is why I did not let you touch her.”**

- **“I know that you did this in the integrity of your heart”:** The Pulpit Commentary clarifies that this does not imply a full divine acquittal—the guilt of the act is implied in the instruction to seek Abraham’s prophetic mediation (v.7). It means “judged from thy moral standpoint,” God recognised Abimelech’s subjective innocence. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik: “Because Abimelech’s heart was right in this regard, God kept him from worse sin. God’s protecting power can guide even a pagan king (Proverbs 21:1).” He adds: “Despite Abraham’s failure to really trust God in the situation, God did not abandon him.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

- **Traditional Protestant application:** God’s restraining grace keeps people from sins they would otherwise commit. This is often cited as an example of “common grace”—God restraining sin even in unbelievers. Matthew Henry: “It is a great mercy to be hindered from committing sin; of this God must have the glory.” (Referenced in https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-20-commentary)

---

## Verse 7

**“Now return the man’s wife, for he is a prophet; he will pray for you and you will live. But if you do not restore her, be aware that you will surely die—you and all who belong to you.”**

- **First use of “prophet” (nabi) in Scripture:** The term comes from a root meaning “to cause to bubble up” or “to pour forth,” applied to one who speaks by divine afflatus. The office of the prophet was twofold: to announce God’s will to men, and to intercede with God for men. This is the first explicit reference to a prophet in the OT. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Dr. Constable notes: “Moses identified Abraham here as a ‘prophet.’ This is the first explicit reference to a prophet in the Old Testament. Prophets received direct revelations from God, spoke to others for God, and praised God (1 Chronicles 25:1). Here the role of the prophet includes that of intercessor, as it does elsewhere in Scripture.” (From search excerpt: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-20.html)

- **Abraham’s intercessory role:** Even though Abraham was presently in sin, he remained a prophet. Guzik: “God’s mercy did not leave Abraham, even though Abraham didn’t trust God the way he should.” God still identified Abraham as His spokesman and designated intercessor. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

- **“He will pray for you and you will live”:** The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew uses the imperative “live thou” as a strong prophetic assurance (cf. Ps 128:5). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

---

## Verse 8

**Early the next morning Abimelech got up and summoned all his servants; and when he described to them all that had happened, the men were terrified.**

- The Pulpit Commentary notes Abimelech’s rising early was “an evidence of the terror into which he had been cast” and his “earnest desire to carry out the Divine instructions.” His confession to his servants—admitting fault, explaining danger, affirming intention to repair the error—was “a proof of the humility of this God-fearing king” (Lange). That the men were “sore afraid” speaks well of the king’s household that they received it seriously. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Dr. Constable notes the chapter is structured as a chiasm with v.8 as the focal point: Abimelech warning his servants. (From search excerpt)

---

## Verse 9

**Then Abimelech called Abraham and asked, “What have you done to us? How have I sinned against you, that you have brought such tremendous guilt upon me and my kingdom? You have done things to me that should not be done.”**

- The Pulpit Commentary notes Abimelech identifies himself with his people (“what have you done to us?”), and “modestly” allows that he himself may have unwittingly occasioned Abraham’s sin. The gravamen of his accusation is that Abraham led him and his people to offend against God, exposing them to divine penalties. “Thou hast done deeds unto me that ought not to be done” — literally “deeds which ought not to be done thou hast done with me” (cf. Gen 34:7). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik: “It was sad to see that Abimelech (the pagan king) was here in the right while Abraham (the man of God) was in the wrong.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

- JFB: “In what a humiliating plight does the patriarch now appear—he, a servant of the true God, rebuked by a heathen prince. Who would not rather be in the place of Abimelech than of the honored but sadly offending patriarch!” JFB then praises Abimelech’s “dignified attitude”—calmly and justly reproving while respecting Abraham’s person and heaping coals of fire on his head by liberal gifts. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-20.html)

---

## Verse 10

**Abimelech also asked Abraham, “What prompted you to do such a thing?”**

- The Pulpit Commentary notes two possible interpretations of “What sawest thou?”: (1) What had you in view? (Knobel, Delitzsch, Keil, Murphy); or (2) What did you actually see? Did you see any of my people seizing wives and murdering husbands? (Rosenmüller, Speaker’s Commentary). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik: “This was a logical question for Abimelech to ask Abraham. Abraham certainly did not have the Lord in view when he lied and failed to trust God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

---

## Verse 11

**Abraham replied, “I thought to myself, ‘Surely there is no fear of God in this place. They will kill me on account of my wife.’”**

- **Abraham’s first excuse — fear:** Abraham assumed Gerar was godless and dangerous. JFB: “From the horrible vices of Sodom he seems to have taken up the impression that all other cities of Canaan were equally corrupt.” Yet, JFB adds, “what a sad thing when men of the world show a higher sense of honor and a greater abhorrence of crimes than a true worshipper!” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-20.html)

- Guzik: “This was Abraham’s excuse for his sinful deception, but the real problem was that, in this situation, the fear of God wasn’t in Abraham. If he had really respected the Lord, His commandments, His promises, and His protection, then Abraham would have never trusted in his own efforts to keep his family safe.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

- Precept Austin quotes Warren Wiersbe: “Abraham stopped asking ‘What is right?’ and began asking ‘What is safe?’ and this led to his downfall.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-20-commentary)

---

## Verse 12

**“Besides, she really is my sister, the daughter of my father—though not the daughter of my mother—and she became my wife.”**

- **A half-truth:** Sarah was indeed Abraham’s half-sister (same father Terah, different mother). The Pulpit Commentary notes some have argued Sarah was actually Terah’s grand-daughter (Iscah, sister of Lot — Josephus, Augustine, Jerome, Jonathan), or Terah’s adopted niece (Calvin), but “there seems no reason for departing from the statement of the text, that she was her husband’s half-sister.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik: “This was another attempt to justify his lie, by saying it was really the truth. But a half-truth, said with the intent to deceive, is often a whole lie.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

- JFB: “What a poor defense Abraham made. The statement absolved him from the charge of direct and absolute falsehood, but he had told a moral untruth because there was an intention to deceive.” JFB adds: “Honesty is always the best policy.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-20.html)

- **Marriage to a half-sister:** Whedon’s Commentary notes that such marriages were later forbidden under Mosaic law (Lev 18:9, 11; 20:17; Deut 27:22) but “may not have been esteemed unlawful in patriarchal times, and they were common among the heathen nations of antiquity.” (From search excerpt: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/genesis-20.html)

---

## Verse 13

**“So when God had me journey from my father’s house, I said to Sarah, ‘This is how you can show your loyalty to me: Wherever we go, say of me, “He is my brother.”’”**

- **The third excuse — a long-standing arrangement:** Abraham reveals this was not a spur-of-the-moment deception but a premeditated policy they had followed from the beginning of their wanderings. The Pulpit Commentary notes the unusual plural verb with Elohim (“God caused me to wander”) — explained variously as accommodation to Abimelech’s polytheistic viewpoint (Keil), a pluralis majestatis (Kalisch), reference to multiple divine manifestations (Lange), or angels (Calvin). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik (quoting Barnhouse) notes the Hebrew verb for “wander” is significant: “The Hebrew word occurs exactly fifty times in Scripture and never in a good sense. It is used of animals going astray, of a drunken man reeling, or staggering, of sinful seduction, of a prophet’s lies causing the people to err… Abraham used the worst word available.” This was an indirect way of blaming God for the problem. Guzik adds Barnhouse’s suggested proper confession: “Abraham should have said: ‘Forgive me, Abimelech, for dishonoring both you and my God…’” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

---

## Verse 14

**So Abimelech brought sheep and cattle, menservants and maidservants, and he gave them to Abraham and restored his wife Sarah to him.**

- The Pulpit Commentary notes Abimelech’s gifts were meant “to propitiate his favor for the wrong he had suffered,” and contrasts this with Pharaoh’s gifts which were “for the sake of Sarah” (Gen 12:16). Some note the LXX and Samaritan versions insert “a thousand didrachmas” here, conflating this with v.16 — but the two donations are distinguished as Abraham’s gift and Sarah’s gift respectively. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik: “In showing such generosity to Abraham, Abimelech did what Romans 12:20 later described as heaping coals of fire on Abraham’s head. This was somewhat backwards; Abraham should have given gifts to Abimelech because Abraham was in the wrong.” He also notes Abraham accepted these gifts, whereas earlier he had refused gifts from a pagan king (Gen 14:21–24) because he wanted no one to think a man had made him rich. “Here, because of Abraham’s compromise, he found it challenging to reclaim the same high moral ground.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

---

## Verse 15

**And Abimelech said, “Look, my land is before you. Settle wherever you please.”**

- The Pulpit Commentary contrasts this generous offer with Pharaoh, who “hastened his departure from the country” (Gen 12:20). Abimelech’s invitation to “dwell where it pleaseth thee” (literally “in the good in thine eyes”) reflects the king’s righteous character. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

---

## Verse 16

**And he said to Sarah, “See, I am giving your brother a thousand pieces of silver. It is your vindication before all who are with you; you are completely cleared.”**

- **A difficult verse:** The Pulpit Commentary offers extensive discussion of the phrase “covering of the eyes” (כְּסוּת עֵינַיִם). Five interpretations are listed: (1) Abraham himself will be Sarah’s protection, hiding her like a veil from others’ desires; (2) the money is a propitiatory gift to make Sarah overlook the offence; (3) the gift is a declaration of Sarah’s purity, defending her against slander; (4) the money is to purchase a veil to hide her beauty; (5) the money provides the bridal veil that married women should always wear (cf. Gen 24:65). “The exact sense of this difficult passage can scarcely be said to have been determined,” though the choice lies between (1) and (2). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- **“Thus she was rebuked”** (or “reproved” / “set right”): The Hebrew וְנֹכָחַת is ambiguous. If taken as the narrator’s statement, it means Sarah was convicted and left defenceless (Gesenius). If taken as part of Abimelech’s speech, it means “and thou art set right” or “justified” (Delitzsch, Keil, Lange). Guzik notes the word has the idea of “set right,” so “it is debatable if Sarah was set right by Abimelech’s rebuke, or if she was found to be right because of her humble submission.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

- Guzik also notes the likely irony in Abimelech’s reference to Abraham as “your brother.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

---

## Verse 17

**Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech and his wife and his maidservants, so that they could again bear children—**

- **Abraham prays:** Abraham fulfilled the prophetic intercessory role God had identified (v.7). The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew uses “the Elohim” (with the article) — the personal and true God, to whom alone belonged the cure. The healing involved both Abimelech and the women of his household. The malady was one that prevented procreation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik: “Abraham did what God told Abimelech he should do (Genesis 20:7) praying for the restoration of health and fertility to his entire household. The exact ailment that Abimelech, his wife, and female servants suffered from is not explained, but they were healed.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

- Precept Austin notes that Abraham’s prayer for the Philistines fulfills the promise of Gen 12:3 — “all peoples on earth will be blessed through you” — as Abraham acts as a prophetic intercessor for the nations. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-20-commentary)

---

## Verse 18

**for on account of Abraham’s wife Sarah, the LORD had completely closed all the wombs in Abimelech’s household.**

- **Use of “the LORD” (Jehovah):** The Pulpit Commentary notes this is the only verse in the chapter using the covenant name Jehovah rather than Elohim, “ascribed to the fact that it is the covenant God of Sarah who there interposes for her protection.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- The malady was a divinely imposed closure of wombs — preventing conception or producing barrenness (cf. Gen 16:2; Isa 66:9; 1 Sam 1:5–6). The Pulpit Commentary quotes Musculus: “poena convenientissima; quid enim convenientius esse poterat, quam ut amittat, qui ad se rapit aliena” (“a most fitting punishment; for what could be more fitting than that he should lose [offspring], who seizes for himself what belongs to another”). The motive was clearly “to protect the purity of the promised seed.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

- Guzik likewise notes God closed the wombs of Abimelech’s household to protect the promised line. The healing in v.17 reversed this judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

---

## Distinctive Protestant Tradition Readings

I was unable to find specific, distinct readings of this chapter from the approved Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, or Anglican sites that materially differ from the general traditional reading. The sources consulted (Guzik/Enduring Word = Pentecostal/charismatic; Precept Austin = broadly evangelical drawing from many traditions; Pulpit = older Anglican; JFB = Reformed-leaning Presbyterian; Constable = evangelical/Dispensational) all agree substantially on the interpretation:

- Abraham sinned by repeating his earlier deception — a failure of faith.
- God graciously intervened to protect Sarah and the Messianic line.
- Abraham was rebuked by a pagan king, bringing shame on his witness.
- Abraham’s role as prophet included intercessory prayer.
- The chapter demonstrates God’s sovereignty in overruling human failure.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises spiritual warfare — Satan’s attempt to thwart the Messianic line — and the need to deal with besetting sins before receiving blessing. Guzik stresses that God’s power restrains even pagan rulers, and that prophetic intercession releases healing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-20/)

**Reformed/Presbyterian (JFB, Calvin via Pulpit):** Stresses the gravity of Abraham’s sin as distrust of God and the “humiliating plight” of a believer being rebuked by a heathen. JFB emphasises moral lessons: “Honesty is always the best policy.” The Pulpit Commentary notes Calvin’s view that Abraham may have left Mamre due to neighbour hostility. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-20.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

---

## Other Views

### NetBible.org / Modern Scholarship

I was unable to fetch or search the NET Bible notes directly due to tool limits. However, Dr. Constable’s notes (referenced above) reflect modern evangelical scholarship: he notes the chiastic structure of the chapter and Sailhamer’s observation that the two “ancestress in jeopardy” stories (Gen 12 and 20) form “an inner frame around the Abraham cycle” — one at the beginning before the promise begins to unfold, and one immediately before Isaac’s birth. Constable also notes that “the episode is chiefly one of suspense: on the brink of Isaac’s birth-story here is the very Promise put in jeopardy, traded away for personal safety.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-20.html — from search excerpts)

### Catholic and Orthodox

I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org due to tool limits. The Pulpit Commentary does reference several early Church interpretations: Josephus, Augustine, and Jerome held that Sarah was Iscah, the daughter of Haran (Gen 11:29), making her Abraham’s niece rather than half-sister — resolving the difficulty of marriage to a half-sister. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/20.htm)

### Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-Grace

No material from these perspectives was found within the approved source sites for this chapter.
